content: The search strategy was designed to identify relevant studies, but due to limitations in time and resources, only articles published in English were included. This decision was based on the assumption that any research capable of significantly altering the results and conclusions would likely have been published in English. Searches were conducted in January 2015 across several electronic databases, including MEDLINE, MEDLINE In-Process, EMBASE, ERIC, PsycINFO, Science Citation Index, Social Policy and Practice, and the Social Science Citation Index. The search strategies for these databases are detailed in Appendices 1–7. The MEDLINE search strategy was adapted for use across all databases. Studies on this topic are often found in the grey literature. However, while some grey literature is accessible through the databases searched, much of it is not. Given the limited resources available for this review, the decision was made not to pursue additional searches for grey literature. Later, the review team was requested by the WHO to search the SCIELO database using the strategy outlined in Appendix 8. Records retrieved from all searches were managed using EndNote (version X7), where duplicates were removed. After de-duplication, 2,114 records were identified, with an additional four records found in SCIELO, resulting in a total of 2,118 studies. Due to time and resource constraints, the review team could not explore all potential sources of information that might have been included in a more comprehensive systematic review. This would have required searching for unpublished studies, grey literature, and studies published in journals not indexed in major bibliographic databases. The search strategy was developed by Melissa Harden, an Information Specialist at York University, for a systematic review on household crowding for the WHO Housing and Health Guidelines. The intent was to avoid missing any pivotal studies that could significantly impact the findings or conclusions of the systematic review. For 45 papers, it appeared that the authors might be able to provide additional data or analyses relevant to the review. The review team attempted to contact the corresponding authors of these reports, sending reminders when no response was received. However, contact information for two authors could not be located, and no replies were received from 18 authors. Three authors reported that they did not have the requested information, six no longer had access to their datasets, and one was too busy to provide the requested analysis. Five authors responded but had not provided the requested information at the time of writing. One author sent a relevant paper from her colleagues that had not been identified in the searches but requested more time to complete the requested analyses, which had not been received at the time of writing. Two authors conducted additional analyses, and seven provided extra information on their studies. The screening of articles was conducted in two stages. In the first stage, titles and abstracts (where available) of records retrieved from the bibliographic databases were independently reviewed by two reviewers for eligibility. Any doubts led to the record being provisionally included. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer. After the initial searches, the WHO provided the review team with prioritized health outcomes. Of the 444 records identified as potentially eligible at this stage, 237 included at least one priority health measure. The full texts of these potentially relevant articles were retrieved and further assessed for eligibility. This second stage of screening was also conducted independently by two reviewers, with disagreements resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer. Several papers could not be located. Appendix 9 lists the 177 articles excluded, along with reasons for their exclusion. The final number of included studies in 2015 was 60. A flow diagram illustrating the identification of studies is presented in the systematic review. To ensure the systematic review was up-to-date, new searches for eligible studies were conducted in March 2018 to identify articles published on or after January 1, 2015. The original search strategies were used for the following databases: EMBASE, ERIC, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Science Citation Index, Social Science Citation Index, and SCIELO (Appendices 10–16). However, due to access limitations, the search could not be re-run in the Social Policy and Practice database. Records retrieved were checked by two authors, and full texts were sought for all studies judged to be potentially eligible. A total of 5,653 records were retrieved, and after de-duplication, 3,181 articles remained. In total, 105 separate studies were included in the review, of which 102 provided sufficient information for inclusion in the narrative synthesis and GRADE evidence profile. Data extraction for both the original and updated searches was conducted by one reviewer and independently checked by another for consistency. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer. Parameters of interest included the location and date of the study, study design, type and number of participants, details of the exposure and any comparator, results for all reported outcomes, and confounders adjusted for in statistical analyses. Quality assessment was conducted independently by the same reviewers who performed data extraction. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by involving a third reviewer. Risk of Bias (RoB) checklists were selected based on the study designs. A modified version of the CASP criteria (2013) was used to assess cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional studies. Additionally, GRADE evidence profile tables were created to evaluate the RoB based on criteria such as consistency of outcome reporting, directness of evidence, precision of results, confounding factors, and overall quality of evidence. The findings of the review are detailed for each outcome, with results reported narratively and tabulated where appropriate. A summary of the characteristics of the included studies is presented in Appendix 17. Five outcomes were considered relevant for this review: tuberculosis (Outcome 1a), other infectious diseases (Outcome 1b), gastroenteritis and diarrheal diseases (Outcome 2), mental health including stress (Outcomes 3 and 5), and sleep disorders (Outcome 4). The quality assessment of the included studies is detailed based on their respective designs, and the interpretation of these findings is also presented. Given the volume of evidence, findings were reported using GRADE evidence profile tables within the main body of the report. These tables provide a detailed assessment of the review outcomes in terms of RoB, inconsistency, indirectness, overall quality, and the importance of the study results to the WHO guideline development team. A summary of the RoB for the studies is presented in Tables 3–7, and GRADE evidence profile tables for each outcome are included in Appendix 18. For Outcome 1a (tuberculosis), 23 studies were included, with at least half being of acceptable quality. Most studies addressed a clearly focused issue and accounted for important confounding factors in their analyses, with some exceptions. The analysis of confounders was not clearly explained in a few studies, and some studies only had abstracts available. In most studies, the sample was recruited acceptably, and both exposure and outcome were measured accurately to minimize bias. However, some studies did not clearly report these domains. Approximately one-fifth of the studies provided a clear explanation of how the sample size was determined, while others provided partial descriptions or did not report this. In at least 80% of the included studies, it was unclear whether the follow-up of subjects was complete or long enough. Overall, most studies provided an adequate description of the statistical analysis and study participants and were considered to have reliable results applicable to the local population. High-quality studies with relatively low RoB included Corbett (2009), Harling and Castro (2013), Hill (2006), Lienhardt (2005), Khan (2016), and Tesema (2015). A summary of the quality assessment for studies reporting on Outcome 1a (TB) is presented in Table 3.
